name: AWS Fargate
summary: Runs ECS tasks and EKS pods without servers: you size each task, AWS finds the machine.
intro: Fargate is a launch type for Amazon ECS and a compute option for Amazon EKS. Instead of running a fleet of EC2 instances for your containers, you set CPU and memory on each ECS task (or EKS pod) and AWS places it on capacity it manages. ECS task sizes run from 0.25 vCPU with 512 MiB up to 32 vCPU with 244 GB on Linux (EKS pods top out at 16 vCPU and 120 GB), and an ECS task gets 20 GiB of ephemeral disk, expandable to 200 GiB.

Each task or pod runs in its own isolated virtual environment (the EKS docs call it a VM), so it doesn’t share a kernel, CPU, memory or network interface with other tasks. Every task gets its own network interface and IP address in your VPC. You pay per second for the vCPU and memory you asked for (one-minute minimum on Linux), and Fargate Spot runs interruptible ECS tasks at up to 70% off.
strengths: No nodes to patch, scale or pack; you never see or SSH into a host
VM-level isolation per task or pod, stronger than containers sharing a node
Works with the ECS and EKS tooling you already use, including load balancers and service autoscaling
Fargate Spot makes batch and other interruptible ECS work much cheaper
limits: No privileged containers, no host networking, and only `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` can be added
On EKS: no DaemonSets, no GPUs, no EBS volumes, no Fargate Spot, and private subnets only
You pay for each task’s full requested size; a steady, dense workload is usually cheaper packed onto EC2 nodes you run yourself
Without a SOCI index, a task downloads its whole image before it starts, so large images start slowly

story: Amazon ECS let teams schedule containers, but only onto EC2 instances they launched, patched, scaled and paid for themselves. Running containers still meant owning “the availability, capacity, and maintenance of the underlying infrastructure”, in the words of AWS’s launch post.

Andy Jassy introduced AWS Fargate at re:Invent on November 29, 2017. It started as a new launch type for ECS in one region, US East (N. Virginia), billed per second for the vCPU and memory each task asked for, with Kubernetes support promised for later. That arrived in December 2019, when EKS could run pods on Fargate, alongside Fargate Spot at up to 70% off. AWS sums up its security model as “every container is wrapped in a virtual machine”, which it says appealed to large financial institutions; Goldman Sachs and Vanguard are among its users.

Fargate turned “serverless containers” into an everyday option: the same images you would run on a cluster, with no cluster to look after. Since then it has mostly grown bigger and broader, adding Arm and Windows in 2021 and 32-vCPU tasks in 2026.

choices.choice: Pay for the task’s size, not for instances
choices.why: You declare CPU and memory per task or pod and pay for exactly that, so there’s no half-empty instance to pay for and each workload’s cost is visible on its own.

choices.choice: Each task in its own virtual machine
choices.why: Containers on a shared host share a kernel. Giving every task its own VM puts a hardware boundary between customers, the property AWS says won over security-conscious users such as banks.

choices.choice: A launch type inside ECS and EKS
choices.why: Rather than a new orchestrator, Fargate replaced only the machines underneath. Teams keep their task definitions or Kubernetes manifests and simply stop managing instances.
Fargate didn’t need Docker’s CLI or image builder. The leaner containerd kept less state, accepted network setups created outside it, and let AWS add features through plugins.

timeline.text: Announced at re:Invent on November 29 as an ECS launch type
Prices cut by up to 50%; EKS support and Fargate Spot in December
Platform version 1.4 switches to containerd and adds EFS volumes
Windows containers and Arm-based Graviton2 support
Task sizes quadruple to 16 vCPU and 120 GB of memory
32-vCPU tasks with up to 244 GiB of memory arrive in June
